claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness in HEAs is governed by the interplay between lattice distortion and deformation mechanisms.
Dislocation motion and twinning are influenced by compositional complexity and microstructural state.
The initial alloy is a single-phase FCC HEA with a homogeneous microstructure.
One principal element will be replaced by an element with a significantly different atomic radius while the alloy remains equiatomic.
Samples will be tested at room temperature under uniaxial tensile loading with similar grain sizes and processing histories.
Atomic size mismatch controls lattice distortion.
Changes in lattice distortion alter stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy affects the activation of dislocation slip, cross-slip, and twinning.
The balance among dislocation slip, cross-slip, and twinning influences toughness.
Increasing atomic size mismatch will increase lattice distortion.
Increasing lattice distortion will reduce stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault energy will promote twinning over dislocation slip.
Promoting twinning over dislocation slip will improve toughness relative to the lower-mismatch baseline.
The baseline is the original unsubstituted alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch.
The proposed relationship is bounded to FCC HEAs having equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions.
The proposed relationship is bounded to grain sizes larger than a critical size associated with dominance of grain-boundary strengthening effects.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to assess lattice distortion.
Toughness can be operationally measured as the area under the tensile stress-strain curve.
Failure of toughness to increase with atomic size mismatch, or failure of lattice distortion and SFE to correlate with toughness trends, would falsify the hypothesis.
